course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: Welcome to Build a Web Framework from Scratch. Express, Fastify, Hono, they all started with the same question: how does an HTTP request become a response? Most of us use one of these frameworks every day. We write app.get, we pass a function, and somehow a browser on the other side of the world gets a page back. In this course we're going to remove the magic. We'll build our own framework, and I'm going to call it Tern, from the raw bytes up. No Express underneath, no http module either. Just Node's net module, which gives us a plain TCP socket, and everything else we write ourselves. Let me show you what we'll end up with.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: By the last chapter you'll be able to write a file that says const app = createApp, then app.use with a logger, then app.get with a path like slash users slash colon id, and a handler that calls res.json. You'll run it, hit it with curl and with a browser, and it will behave like a real framework. The difference is that you'll know what every line underneath does, and that is the whole point of this course. The course has seven chapters. Chapter one is theory, and it's short: what HTTP actually is, what a request looks like on the wire, and what headers, bodies and status codes mean. Chapter two is where we start typing.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: We open a TCP server with net.createServer, we read the bytes that arrive, and we write a parser that turns them into a request object. Then we send a hand-built response back so a real browser accepts it. Chapter three is the router. We'll start with the naive version, a big if statement matching strings, feel it get slow and ugly, and then replace it with a radix tree, the same family of data structure that fast routers use. We'll add dynamic parameters like colon id and wildcards on top. Chapter four is middleware, the next function pattern that makes Express feel the way it does, including error-handling middleware with four arguments. Chapter five is the friendly layer: a req object with query and params, a res object with status, json and send, and support for HTML and binary responses.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: Chapter six is plugins. We'll design a plugin system, then use it to build two real things: a body parser that reads JSON and form data, and a static file server. Chapter seven is the payoff. We'll look at why Fastify can route so much faster than Express, compare Tern against Express honestly, and talk about where to go next. Along the way I'll keep the file layout stable: a folder called tern, with server.js, parser.js, router.js, app.js, request.js, response.js, and a plugins folder. Same names all the way through. A few practical things before we start. You need Node 18 or newer, a terminal, and an editor. You should be comfortable with JavaScript functions, closures and a bit of async code. You don't need to know any networking.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: And I'd like you to type along rather than copy, because the bugs you hit are half of the learning. Also, we're going to write code that is clear first and fast second. Tern is a teaching framework, not something you'd deploy for a bank, and I'll tell you honestly where production frameworks do more than we do. Okay. Let's begin where everything begins, with the question of what HTTP even is. Before we write a single line of Tern, I want to answer a question that most tutorials skip: why does HTTP exist? If you understand the problem it solved, the shape of every request and response will feel obvious instead of arbitrary. So let's go back to around 1989.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: Tim Berners-Lee is at CERN, and physicists there keep their notes and papers on lots of different computers, in different formats. Finding anything means logging in somewhere and knowing where to look. His idea was a web of linked documents, where a document on one machine can point at a document on another machine. For that idea to work you need three things. You need a way to name a document, which became the URL. You need a format for the document that can contain links, which became HTML. And you need a way for one computer to ask another computer for a document, and that is HTTP, the HyperText Transfer Protocol. Notice how small the original job was.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: A client says, give me this document, and a server says, here it is, or sorry, I don't have it. That's the whole idea. The first version, now called HTTP 0.9, was almost embarrassingly simple. The client opened a connection, sent one line that looked like GET slash index.html, and the server sent back the HTML and closed the connection. No headers, no status codes, no content types. Only HTML could be returned, because there was no way to say anything else. If something went wrong, the server just sent back an HTML page describing the error. A human read it. Nothing else needed to understand it. That couldn't last, because people wanted images, and they wanted to know whether a request had worked without reading prose.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: So HTTP 1.0 added the pieces we use today: a version on the request line, headers on both sides, and a status code at the start of the response. Then HTTP 1.1 in 1997 added the thing that matters most for us: persistent connections, so a client can send several requests down the same TCP connection, plus the Host header, which let many websites share one server. Now, an important design choice. HTTP is a text protocol that sits on top of TCP. TCP gives you a reliable stream of bytes between two programs. It doesn't know what a request is, it doesn't know where one message ends and the next begins. HTTP is the agreement about how to cut that stream into messages.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 1.1 - What is HTTP and Why It Was Invented
text: That's why we can build a web server out of net.createServer: we get the stream, and we apply the agreement ourselves. The second design choice is that HTTP is stateless. Every request must carry everything the server needs to answer it. The server doesn't remember that you asked something a second ago. That sounds like a limitation, but it's why the web scales: any server in a fleet can answer any request. Cookies and sessions are later additions, built on top of headers, and later we'll see how a framework like Tern can offer them as a plugin. Last point for this lecture. HTTP is a request and response protocol where the client always speaks first. The server never sends something unprompted. Keep that picture in your head: a client sends a message, the server sends exactly one message back. In the next lecture we'll look at the exact characters of those messages, the wire format, and I promise it's more readable than you expect.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Let me show you what HTTP looks like on the wire, because this is what our framework will be reading and writing. Open a terminal. Make sure you have curl, which ships with macOS and most Linux systems. Run curl with the dash v flag against any plain http site, for example example.com. Lines starting with a greater-than sign are what curl sent. Lines starting with a less-than sign are what came back. This is the wire format, with a bit of decoration. Here's the first thing you'll see. The request starts with a line: GET slash HTTP slash 1.1. That's the request line, and it has exactly three parts separated by single spaces. The method, which says what you want to do.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The target, usually a path, possibly with a query string. And the protocol version. Remember these three parts, because the first function we write in parser.js will split exactly this line. Below the request line come headers. Each header is a name, a colon, and a value, one per line. Host: example.com. User-Agent: curl. Accept: star slash star. Header names are case-insensitive, which will matter when we store them, so we'll lowercase them. Then comes a blank line. And that blank line is the single most important character sequence in HTTP, because it's what tells the receiver: the headers are over. Now, what exactly separates those lines? Not a plain newline. HTTP uses carriage return followed by line feed, written backslash r backslash n, usually called CRLF.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So the real bytes of our request are: G E T space slash space H T T P slash 1.1, then backslash r backslash n, then Host colon space example.com, backslash r backslash n, and finally one more backslash r backslash n by itself. The end of headers is backslash r backslash n backslash r backslash n. Write that down. We'll search for that exact four-character sequence in our code. The response has the same shape. First a status line: HTTP slash 1.1, a space, 200, a space, OK. Version, status code, and a reason phrase. Then headers, such as Content-Type: text slash html and Content-Length: 1256. Then the blank line. Then the body, which is the raw bytes of the page.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So both directions are: a start line, headers, a blank line, and optionally a body. How does the receiver know where the body ends? That's the other critical question, since TCP is just a stream. There are two common answers. One is the Content-Length header: it says the body is exactly this many bytes, so read that many and stop. The other is chunked transfer encoding, where the body is sent in pieces, each prefixed by its size. In Tern we'll support Content-Length, and I'll point out later where chunked would plug in. Why do I make such a fuss about this? Because every framework feature we build, routing, middleware, JSON helpers, is a convenience layer on top of three small things: a request line, headers, and a body.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If you can see those three things, nothing in the framework is mysterious. Next, let's look more closely at headers, bodies and status codes. A quick way to feel all this is to skip curl entirely and use netcat. Run nc example.com 80, type GET slash HTTP slash 1.1, press enter, type Host colon example.com, press enter twice, and the server answers you right there in the terminal. You've just been an HTTP client by hand. One gotcha: some terminals send a plain newline instead of CRLF, and strict servers will complain. That small annoyance is a preview of why our parser has to be careful about the exact bytes it receives, and why we won't trust anything we read off the socket.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Last lecture we saw that every HTTP message is a start line, headers, a blank line and an optional body. Now let's spend time on the three pieces that carry meaning: headers, the body, and the status code. These are the vocabulary our framework will expose to the people using it, so I want you to have each of them clear before we start parsing. Let's start with headers. A header is metadata about the message, a name and a value. Some describe the sender: User-Agent says what software is making the request, Host says which website it wants. Some negotiate: Accept says what formats the client understands, Accept-Encoding says whether it can handle gzip.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Some describe the body: Content-Type says what the bytes are, such as application slash json or text slash html, and Content-Length says how many there are. And some carry state: Cookie on the way in, Set-Cookie on the way out. Two details will bite us later, so let me say them now. First, header names are case-insensitive. Content-Type, content-type and CONTENT-TYPE are the same header. When we parse, we'll store every name in lowercase, and when users call req.get, we'll lowercase what they ask for. Second, the same header can appear more than once. Set-Cookie is the classic case, where a server sends several cookies as separate header lines. Our first parser will keep it simple and overwrite duplicates, but I'll flag where a more careful framework joins them or keeps an array.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Now the body. A GET request usually has no body, since you're asking for something. A POST or PUT usually has one, since you're sending something: a JSON object, form fields, a file upload. The server's response has a body too, normally the thing you asked for. Remember that the body is just bytes. HTTP doesn't care if it's text or an image. That is why Content-Type exists, and why in the body parser lecture in chapter six we'll decide how to interpret the bytes based on that header. The status code is a three digit number at the start of every response, and its first digit tells you the category. The one hundreds are informational, which you rarely see.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The two hundreds mean success: 200 OK, 201 Created when you made something, 204 No Content when there's nothing to send back. The three hundreds are redirects: 301 means moved permanently, 302 and 307 are temporary, and 304 Not Modified is the cache saying you already have the latest copy. The four hundreds mean the client made a mistake. 400 Bad Request when the message is malformed. 401 when you aren't authenticated, 403 when you are but aren't allowed. 404 Not Found, the most famous one, which our router will return when nothing matches. 405 Method Not Allowed when the path exists but not for that method. And the five hundreds mean the server failed: 500 Internal Server Error, which our error-handling middleware will produce, and 503 when the service is unavailable.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Why does the first digit matter so much? Because clients, caches and proxies make decisions from it without understanding the specific code. A browser retries or shows an error depending on the category. So when you design your own API, choose codes honestly: return 404 when a thing doesn't exist, not 200 with a message saying error. Your own tooling and everyone else's will thank you. You now have the whole vocabulary: a method and a target, a version, headers, a body, and a status. That's enough theory. In chapter two we write code. We'll open a TCP server with net.createServer, look at the raw buffers that arrive when curl connects, and start turning them into something our framework can use. Grab your editor and make an empty folder called tern. See you in the next lecture.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Alright, time to write code. Open your tern folder and create a file called server.js. This is the very bottom of our framework, the part that talks to the network. And I want to start by being clear about what we're not using. Node ships with an http module, and Express is built on it, but http already parses requests for us. That would defeat the purpose. Instead we use the net module, which gives us TCP sockets and nothing more. So at the top I'll write const net equals require of net. net has one function that matters right now: net.createServer. You give it a callback, and Node calls that callback every time a client connects, passing in a socket.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: A socket is a duplex stream, meaning you can read bytes from it and write bytes to it. So let me write it. const server equals net.createServer, then an arrow function taking socket. Inside, I'll just log a line saying a client connected. After that, server.listen, port 3000, and a callback that logs listening on 3000. Save it and run node server.js. Nothing happens, and that's correct. The server is waiting. Open a second terminal and run curl dash v localhost colon 3000. Look at the first terminal: client connected. And look at curl, it's hanging. That's actually informative. curl connected, sent its request, and is now waiting for a response that we never send. Press control C in curl to stop it.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We've proved that the TCP connection works, and that a browser or curl treats us as a real server. Now let's see what they sent. A socket emits a data event whenever bytes arrive, so inside the callback I'll write socket.on, the string data, and a function taking chunk. The chunk is a Buffer, which is Node's type for raw bytes. If I log it directly I get a hex dump, which isn't friendly, so I'll log chunk.toString, the string utf8. Run curl again, and there it is: GET slash HTTP slash 1.1, then Host: localhost colon 3000, User-Agent: curl and Accept: star slash star. Exactly the wire format from chapter one. Let me make the CRLFs visible, because this is important.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Instead of printing the string, print JSON.stringify of chunk.toString. Now you'll see backslash r backslash n at the end of each line, and at the end, the double backslash r backslash n that marks the end of the headers. This is our proof that the lecture material wasn't theory. The bytes really look like that. One more concept before we move on. Data events are not requests. A data event just means some bytes arrived. A small request normally arrives in one chunk, but a large POST with a big body might arrive in several, and the opposite is possible too: with keep-alive, a client can send two requests so quickly that they arrive glued together in one chunk.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: TCP is a stream and gives no promise about boundaries. So our server can never assume that one data event equals one request. We have to accumulate bytes and look for the end of headers ourselves. Let me also handle two small things so our server doesn't crash. Sockets emit an error event, for instance when a client resets the connection, and an unhandled error event on an emitter throws and kills the process. So I'll add socket.on error with a handler that simply destroys the socket. And I'll wrap the whole thing in a function. We'll export a function createServer that takes a handler, so later app.js can call it. For now, move the net.createServer code inside it and return the server. Next lecture: we turn those chunks into a request object.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Last time we got raw bytes arriving on a socket. Now we turn them into a request object. Create a new file called parser.js. I want this to be a pure function with no networking in it, because pure functions are easy to test and reason about. The signature is parseRequest, taking a buffer, and returning either null, meaning not enough bytes yet, or an object with the parsed request and how many bytes it consumed. Step one is to find the end of the headers. Buffers have an indexOf method that accepts a string, so I write const headEnd equals buffer.indexOf of backslash r backslash n backslash r backslash n. If that returns minus one, we haven't received all the headers yet, so we return null and wait for more data.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Otherwise, the head is everything before that index. I'll write const head equals buffer.subarray of zero to headEnd, dot toString of latin1. I choose latin1 deliberately: header bytes are treated as single-byte characters, and it never throws on odd input. Step two is the request line and headers. I split the head on backslash r backslash n. The first element is the request line, and I split that on a space to get method, target and version. If any of the three is missing, we should throw an error with a status of 400, since that's a malformed request. Notice I'm picking the error shape now: an Error with a statusCode property. Our server will catch it and send that status back. Step three is the headers.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: For every remaining line, I find the first colon with indexOf. Everything before is the name, everything after is the value. I lowercase the name and trim the value, then store it in a plain object. Why the first colon? Because values can contain colons, like Host: localhost colon 3000. If I split on every colon I'd cut that value in half. It's a classic bug, and it's good to hit it once on purpose, so try splitting on all colons and watch the Host header break. Step four is the target. A request target like slash users question mark page equals two includes the query string. I'll split it at the question mark into pathname and query. We'll parse the query properly in chapter five, so for now I keep the raw string.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So far parseRequest returns method, path, query, version and headers. Step five is the body. I read headers.content-length, which is a string, and convert it with Number. If it's missing, the length is zero. The body starts at headEnd plus four, since the separator is four bytes, and ends at that start plus length. If the buffer doesn't yet contain that many bytes, we return null again and wait. If it does, body is buffer.subarray of start to end, and the total consumed is end. Returning consumed matters: anything after it belongs to the next request on the same connection. Now wire it into server.js. In the connection callback I keep a variable called pending, starting as an empty Buffer.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: On every data event, I set pending to Buffer.concat of pending and chunk, then call parseRequest in a loop. While the result isn't null, I hand the request to the user's handler and cut the consumed bytes off pending. A try and catch around it turns a thrown 400 into a response. Test with curl, and with curl dash d for a POST body. You should see your parsed object logged, method, path, headers, body and all. One last honest note about limits. A real server caps the size of the headers and the body, otherwise a client can send an endless stream and exhaust memory. We'll add a simple maximum later. For now, the parser works. Next, we answer.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Our server can now read requests, but curl is still hanging because we never reply. In this lecture we send a response, and we'll do it completely by hand, so you see that a response is also just a string. Open server.js. Right now the handler logs the parsed request. Let's replace that with a function that writes bytes to the socket. Remember the response shape: a status line, headers, a blank line, then the body. I'll build it in the simplest way possible. const body equals the string hello from Tern. Then const head equals an array of strings joined with backslash r backslash n. The first is HTTP slash 1.1 space 200 space OK.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The second is Content-Type colon text slash plain. The third is Content-Length colon, and here we have a subtle trap. The length must be in bytes, not characters. So I write Buffer.byteLength of body. If your body had an emoji or an accented letter, string length would be wrong and the client would hang or truncate. After the headers I need the blank line, so after joining I add two more CRLFs: the head string, plus backslash r backslash n backslash r backslash n, plus body. Then socket.write of that string. Run it, hit it with curl dash i, which prints response headers too, and you get your first real answer: HTTP slash 1.1 200 OK, the headers, and hello from Tern.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Open it in a browser too. It renders. A browser can't tell our server from nginx. Now, what happens if we forget Content-Length? Try it: remove that line. The browser still shows the text, but the page keeps loading, because the client doesn't know whether more bytes are coming. It's waiting for the connection to close. This tells us there are two honest ways to finish a response: tell the client the length, or close the connection. Let me show the second. I'll add a header Connection colon close, and after writing, call socket.end. Now the request completes, because the socket closing is the signal. That raises the keep-alive question. HTTP 1.1 connections are persistent by default, which saves a new TCP handshake for every request.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: For Tern, I'll support both modes in a simple way: if the request has Connection: close, we end the socket after replying; otherwise we leave it open and keep parsing, which our loop from last lecture already supports. Always sending Content-Length makes this safe, and that's why I insisted on it. Let's tidy this into a reusable function, because soon response.js will own this job. I'll write a function called writeResponse taking socket, status, headers and body. It looks up the reason phrase from a small object: 200 OK, 201 Created, 400 Bad Request, 404 Not Found, 500 Internal Server Error. It adds Content-Length automatically from the body, and joins everything.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Now the handler becomes a single call, and the 400 from our parser uses the same function with the error's statusCode. Try curl with a broken request, using printf piped into nc, and check you receive a 400. Quick recap of chapter two. We have server.js, which accepts connections and accumulates bytes, parser.js, which turns bytes into a request object, and a function that writes a response. That is a working HTTP server in about eighty lines, with no http module. Everything from here on is about making this pleasant to use. And the very first thing that gets unpleasant is routing: our handler can't tell slash from slash users. So chapter three starts there, with the naive way to do it.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Our server can read a request and write a response, but every request currently gets the same answer. A framework needs routing: when the request is GET slash users, run this function; when it's POST slash users, run that one. In this lecture we build the simplest possible router, on purpose, and then we measure where it falls over. That's how we earn the right to use a smarter data structure in the next lecture. Create router.js. The simplest design is an array. I'll write class Router, with a constructor that sets this.routes to an empty array. Then a method add, taking method, path and handler, which pushes an object with those three fields. And a method find, taking method and path. Inside, a for loop over this.routes: if route.method equals method and route.path equals path, return route.handler.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If nothing matches, return null. That's the whole router. In server.js, build a router, add a route for GET slash that sends hello, add GET slash about, and have the handler call find. When it returns null, we send a 404. Run it and test. Slash works, slash about works, slash nope gives 404. Great. That's a real router, and honestly for five routes it's perfectly fine. Never let anyone tell you that you must start with a clever structure. But let's look at what we can't do yet. Real apps have paths like slash users slash 42, slash users slash 43, and so on. We can't register infinitely many exact strings. We need patterns. First attempt: patterns as strings, split on slashes. When adding slash users slash colon id, I split into the segments users and colon id.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: When finding slash users slash 42, I split it into users and 42, loop over every route, compare segment counts, then compare segment by segment: if the route segment starts with a colon, it matches anything and saves the value into a params object; otherwise it must match exactly. That works. Let me wire it up and try slash users slash 42. We get params with id equal to 42. Now let's measure. Add a thousand routes in a loop, with paths like slash resource slash number slash items, then register the one we care about last, and call find in a loop a million times, timing it with console.time. You'll see that cost grows with route count: each lookup walks the list from the top, splitting strings and comparing segments for every route before reaching ours.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Double the routes, roughly double the time. Computer scientists call this linear time, O of n. Is that actually a problem? Be honest here. A request involves network, parsing, probably a database call that takes milliseconds. The routing cost for fifty routes is microseconds. So the naive router is not wrong because it's slow today. It's wrong because the cost scales with a number we don't control, the size of the app, and because every request pays it. Express actually works like this, a linear scan of a stack, and it gets by perfectly well. We're doing better for two other reasons: it's instructive, and it's what lets frameworks like Fastify advertise routing numbers that are a different league. There are also correctness problems lurking. In our array version, the order of registration decides who wins.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If I register slash users slash colon id before slash users slash me, then slash users slash me gets captured by the parameter route, and the specific route is dead code. A good router should prefer the most specific match no matter the order. And we split strings on every request, allocating arrays and garbage. A smarter structure can do all the work at registration time, and almost none during lookup. So here's what we want. Lookup cost independent of route count, in other words proportional to the length of the path being looked up. Static routes beat parameter routes beat wildcards, automatically. Parameter extraction with no regular expressions. The structure that gives us all of that is a tree where routes that share a beginning share nodes, and that's the radix tree we build next lecture. Keep the naive router around, because we'll use it as a baseline to benchmark against.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Let's talk about the data structure. Take these routes: slash users, slash users slash settings, slash user slash list, and slash about. Many of them begin with the same characters. A trie, also called a prefix tree, exploits that. Each node represents one character, and a route is a path down from the root. The routes share nodes for their shared beginnings, so looking up slash users slash settings means walking down exactly one node per character, never comparing against slash about at all. Lookup cost depends on the length of the path, not on the number of routes. A plain trie has one problem: it's wasteful. A node per character means a chain of single-child nodes for every long route.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So we use a radix tree, also called a compressed trie. The rule is simple: if a node has exactly one child and isn't itself the end of a route, merge it with that child, and store a whole string on each edge. Instead of nodes for s, e, t, t, i, n, g, s, you have one node holding the string settings. Fewer nodes, fewer jumps, better cache behaviour. Let's build it in router.js. First, class RadixNode. The constructor takes a prefix string, and sets this.prefix, this.children as an empty array, and this.handler as null. Children as an array is fine for now. Faster implementations index children by first character, and I'll show that trick at the end.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Then in Router, replace the routes array with this.trees, an object that maps an HTTP method to the root node. Each method gets its own tree, so a GET lookup never searches POST routes. Now insertion, the interesting part. Write insert, taking node, path, handler. We look through the node's children for one that shares a first character with path. If none does, we create a new child with the whole remaining path as its prefix, attach the handler, and we're done. If one does, we compute the length of the common prefix between path and the child's prefix, using a small loop that compares characters. Three cases follow. Case one: the common prefix equals the child's whole prefix.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The child fully matches, so we strip that part off our path and recurse into the child. If nothing remains, we've arrived, and we set the handler there. Case two: the common prefix is shorter than the child's prefix. We have to split the child. Say the child holds slash users and we're inserting slash user slash list. The common part is slash user. We create a new node with prefix slash user, give the old child the remainder, which is s, and make it a child of the new node, and then insert the rest of our path under the new node. That split step is the heart of the radix tree. Case three is the one people forget: inserting a route that ends exactly at a split point.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If I register slash user and the tree has slash users, the split creates a node for slash user, and since our path is now empty, that new node receives the handler. Let me trace it in the debugger together. Register slash users, then slash user, then slash user slash list, and print the tree with a little recursive function using indentation. You should see slash user at the top, with children s and slash list. Now lookup. find takes method and path, grabs the tree for that method, and walks. At each node, we look for a child whose prefix is a prefix of the remaining path, using startsWith with an offset. If found, we move into it and consume that many characters.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: When the remaining path is empty and the node has a handler, we return it. If there's no matching child, we return null, and the server answers 404. Test it with your four routes. Then rerun the benchmark from last lecture, with a thousand routes. The difference is dramatic, and it stays flat as we add routes. Before we move on, there's one performance refinement worth knowing. Instead of looping over children to find a match, real routers store a string of the children's first characters, indices, and use indexOf on it to jump straight to the right child. We keep the array for readability, but the idea is that lookup does almost no work per character. In the next lecture we make the tree understand dynamic segments.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Right now our radix tree only understands literal text. But real routes look like slash users slash colon id slash posts slash colon postId, and slash static slash star. In this lecture we add dynamic parameters and wildcards to the tree in router.js, without giving up its speed. First, the design decision. There are three kinds of segments in a path: static text, a parameter that matches one segment, and a wildcard that matches everything left. A node should know which kind it is. So I'll add a field to RadixNode called type, with the values static, param and wildcard. The constructor defaults to static. For param nodes, I also store the parameter name, such as id, in a field called paramName.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Wildcard nodes keep the name star. How do we insert? Before inserting a path, I split it at the first colon or star. Take slash users slash colon id slash posts. Everything before the colon, slash users slash, is static text and goes through the radix insert we already wrote. Then the colon begins a param: we read the name up to the next slash, so id. We create a param node as a child of the last static node, and continue inserting the remainder, slash posts, beneath it. A star becomes a wildcard node and ends the route, since it swallows everything after it. Where do we keep these special children? On the node, I add two extra fields: paramChild and wildcardChild, separate from the normal children array.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That's a clean way to give static children priority without sorting anything. Now we get the specificity guarantee I promised two lectures ago: slash users slash me is a static child, slash users slash colon id is the paramChild, and lookup always tries the static children first. Registration order stops mattering. Now the lookup. The function becomes recursive, with signature search of node, path, params. Step one: try the static children, as before. If a static child matches, recurse into it, and if that recursion returns a result, return it. Step two, if there was no static result, try paramChild. Find the end of the segment, the next slash or the end of the path. The text up to there is the parameter value.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Store it, params at paramChild.paramName equals that value, and recurse with the rest of the path. Step three, try the wildcard: store the entire remaining path as params star and return its handler. Notice what that order buys us, and also what it costs. Because we try static, then param, then wildcard, if a static branch goes down and fails later, we backtrack and try the param branch. For slash users slash me slash posts, imagine only slash users slash colon id slash posts is registered. The static branch me doesn't exist, so we go straight to param. But if me exists with different children, a failed static attempt must delete any params it set, so I'll clean up on the way back.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Backtracking is cheap here because trees are shallow. Let me test everything. Register GET slash users slash me, GET slash users slash colon id, GET slash users slash colon id slash posts slash colon postId, and GET slash files slash star. Then call find for slash users slash me, which returns the me handler with empty params. Slash users slash 42 returns params id 42. Slash users slash 42 slash posts slash 7 returns id 42 and postId 7. Slash files slash a slash b slash c.txt returns star equal to a slash b slash c.txt. And slash users slash 42 slash nothing gives null. Two edge cases to decide consciously. Trailing slashes: is slash users the same as slash users slash?

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Express treats them the same by default; many routers don't. I'll normalize by stripping a trailing slash, except for the root. And decoding: a parameter value like hello%20world should be run through decodeURIComponent, inside a try and catch, because malformed escapes throw, and that should be a 400. We'll return the decoded value. That finishes the router. Our find function returns a handler and a params object, and the server can finally dispatch properly. But look at the handler's shape: every handler is called with raw socket-ish stuff. Chapter four fixes that by introducing middleware, the pipeline that every request flows through before it reaches a handler.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We have a server, a parser and a router. Now picture what a real application needs to do on every request. Log the method and path. Check whether the user is logged in. Parse a JSON body. Add CORS headers. Time how long the request takes. Only after all that does your actual handler run. If you pasted that code into every handler you'd have a mess. Middleware is the answer, and it's the single idea that defines Express, Koa, Hono and nearly everything like them. Here's the definition I want you to carry. A middleware is a function that sits in the middle of the request and response. It receives the request, the response, and a function called next.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: It can do some work, then either end the response itself, or call next to hand control to whatever comes after it. That's it. A chain of such functions forms a pipeline, and each one decides whether the request continues. Let me draw the idea as an onion, because it's helpful. The request enters from outside. The first middleware, say the logger, sees it first. Then the authentication check, then the body parser, then finally the route handler at the center. The response travels back out through the same layers in reverse, if the middleware wants to act afterwards, for example to log how long it took. Each layer wraps the next, and the layers don't know about each other.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That separation is what makes middleware composable. Let's start building it, in a new file called app.js. This will be the public face of Tern: what users import. I'll write function createApp, which creates a local array called stack, and returns an app object. The first method is app.use, which takes a function and pushes it onto the stack. The second is app.listen, which takes a port, and calls the createServer function from server.js with a handler named handle. Right now, handle is an empty function, but we'll fill it in the next lecture. Why an array and not something fancier? Because order is the entire feature. Middleware runs in the order you registered it.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If the body parser comes after your route handler, the handler sees no body. If the logger is registered last, it never logs requests that were already answered by earlier middleware. This is the first thing people get wrong in Express, and it's also why you'll see app.use calls at the top of every Express file. Let me show what the user code will look like, so we're building toward something concrete. const app equals createApp. Then app.use of a function taking req, res and next that logs req.method and req.url, then calls next. Then another app.use that sets a header. Then app.get of slash, with a handler that sends hello. Notice the logger doesn't know about the route, and the route doesn't know about the logger.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We'll make that exact file run at the end of the next lecture. One design question we should settle now: should middleware support paths? Express lets you write app.use of slash admin, and a function, so the function only runs for URLs under slash admin. That's convenient. We'll support it simply: use accepts an optional first argument that's a string prefix. When the request path starts with that prefix, the middleware runs; otherwise it's skipped. Our stack entries will be objects with a prefix and a fn. I'd keep exact semantics modest, since prefix matching has edge cases, such as slash admin matching slash administrator. We'll check for a slash boundary. Next lecture: the machinery behind next.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The core of middleware is a dozen lines, and it confuses almost everyone the first time, so let's go slowly. Open app.js. We have a stack of entries, and we want to run them one after another, where each can call next to continue. The trick is to write a function called dispatch, that takes an index, and runs the entry at that index, giving it a next function that calls dispatch with index plus one. Let me write it. Inside handle, which receives req and res, I declare let index equals negative one. Then function next, with an optional error argument. Inside it, index plus plus. Then const entry equals stack at index. If there's no entry, we've run out of middleware. Then entry.fn gets called with req, res and next.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That's the whole pattern, and the closure over index is the clever part: next is the same function each time, but it advances a shared counter. Why this works is worth a moment. When the first middleware calls next, that call runs the second middleware synchronously, inside the first one's call stack. When the second one finishes, we return into the first, which may run code after its next call. That's exactly the onion: code before next is the way in, code after next is the way out. If the middleware is async, it can await things, and the return path happens later, which we'll deal with. Now what do we do when the stack runs out? That's the final step in the story. If the request got through every middleware and nobody ended the response, the answer is 404.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So when entry is undefined, we send a 404 with the text Not Found. But where does our router fit? Here's the cleanest approach: the router is itself just a middleware, the last one in the stack. It looks up the method and path, and if there's a match, it sets req.params and calls the handler. If not, it calls next, and we fall off the end into the 404. So app.get of path, handler registers the route in the router. And in createApp I push a single router middleware at the end when listening, or better, when handle is built, so user middleware registered after the routes still runs first, in the order the users placed it. A clean and common choice is to run all app.use entries first and the router last. I'll go with that and document it.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Chapter six will show a different option, where routes can sit in the same ordered stack. Let's test it. Register a logger that prints the method and URL, then calls next. Register a second middleware that sets req.startedAt to Date.now, and calls next. Register GET slash with a handler that writes hello. Run curl and watch: logger prints, route answers. Now deliberately forget to call next in the logger. Curl hangs. This is the number one middleware bug, so burn it in. If a middleware neither responds nor calls next, the request just sits there forever. I'll sometimes add a timeout in production frameworks for exactly this reason. The opposite mistake is just as nasty: calling next twice. The second call advances the index again and runs the following middleware a second time, and you'd get two responses, and a crash writing to a finished socket.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: A defensive version records the highest index it has dispatched, and rejects a call to next with the same one. I'll add that guard: keep a variable called called, check it, and throw an error saying next called multiple times. That's what Koa does and it's a good habit. What about async middleware? If a middleware is an async function, it returns a promise. We should await the result of calling entry.fn, and if the promise rejects, treat that as an error and route it to error handling. So I wrap the call in a try and catch, and use Promise.resolve of the return value, then catch to call next with the error. Now users can write app.use of async req res next and throw freely. That sets the stage for the next lecture: what happens when something goes wrong.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Errors happen. A handler throws because a user sent weird data, a database call fails, a file doesn't exist. What should our framework do? The worst answer is to let the exception escape and crash the process or leave the request hanging. The right answer is the one Express made famous: errors flow through the same pipeline, and special middleware gets a chance to handle them. Express's trick is based on function length. A normal middleware has three parameters: req, res, next. An error-handling middleware has four: err, req, res, next. The framework inspects fn.length, which is the number of declared parameters, and uses that to tell them apart. It's a little strange, honestly, a convention built on reflection, but it's simple, it works everywhere, and it's what we'll copy so Tern feels familiar.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Let's extend the next function in app.js. It now receives an optional err argument. Here's the rule. When next is called with no argument, we move forward and skip any entry whose fn.length is four, since those only care about errors. When next is called with an error, we do the opposite: skip everything with fewer than four parameters, and run only error handlers, passing err first. So the loop becomes a small while loop: find the next entry that's appropriate for the current mode, and run it. Next, where do errors enter? Three places. First, a middleware calls next with an error explicitly, such as next of new Error and a message. Second, a synchronous throw, which our try and catch around entry.fn catches, and forwards using next of the thrown value.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Third, an async function that rejects, which we already convert. All three paths funnel into the same next call, which means one mechanism handles everything. I like that: it's a good example of reducing special cases. What if nobody handles the error? We need a default handler at the end of the chain. When we run out of entries while in error mode, we send a 500 response. If the error has a statusCode, like the 400 our parser throws, or a status field, we use that instead. The body should be a plain message. In development, you might include the stack trace; in production, never leak it. I'll add a simple check on process.env.NODE_ENV. Let me write the default handler as a function at the bottom of app.js, called finalHandler, taking err, req, res.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: It computes the status as err.statusCode if it's a number, otherwise 500. It logs the error with console.error, because swallowed errors are miserable to debug. Then it writes the response. If headers were already sent, we can't change the status; in that case, the only sane move is to close the socket. Check res.headersSent, which we'll implement formally in chapter five. Now try it. Register a route that does throw new Error of boom. Without any handler, curl should show a 500 with Internal Server Error. Next, register an error middleware, app.use of a function with err, req, res and next, that sends status 500 with a JSON object containing the message. Order matters again: error handlers go after the things that can throw.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If you place it first, it never sees the error, since errors only travel forward in the stack. Two more things. Not Found is not an error in our design, it's the natural end of the chain. Some people prefer to create a 404 error and funnel it through handlers so one place formats all failures. It's a design choice; Fastify, for instance, has a dedicated not-found handler. We'll keep ours simple. And chain error handlers: an error handler can call next of err to pass the error to the next error handler, for example to log first and respond later. That finishes middleware. In chapter five, we make req and res pleasant.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Until now our handlers have been working with a raw parsed object, a plain bag of method, path and headers. That's fine for us, but it's not a friendly API. In this lecture we create request.js and give handlers a proper req object, with everything they'd expect: req.method, req.path, req.query, req.params, req.headers, req.get, req.body and req.ip. This is the object people see every day, so its design is a large part of how the framework feels. Open a new file, request.js. I'll write a function createRequest, which takes the parsed request from parser.js and the socket, and returns a new object. Why a function returning a plain object instead of a class? Simplicity, mostly. For a teaching framework, a factory is easier to read.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: But I'll tell you the trade-off: classes with methods on the prototype save memory, since each method exists once, while our factory would create new closures per request. Production frameworks care about this, and later we'll revisit it. Let's fill in the simple fields first. method is copied over. path is the pathname from the parser. url is the original target, including the query string. headers is the lowercase header object. And body starts as undefined, because a body parser will set it later. Then req.get, a method taking a name, which returns this.headers at name lowercased. So req.get of Content-Type works regardless of how the user capitalizes it. That's a tiny function, but it's the reason we lowercased header names in the parser. Now the query string.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The parser gave us the raw string after the question mark, for example page equals two and sort equals asc. Node has a built-in URLSearchParams class, which we can use. I'll write const query equals Object.fromEntries of new URLSearchParams of the raw string. That gives us an object with page as the string two and sort as asc. Notice the values are strings, always. If a user needs a number they must convert, and I think that's right: the framework shouldn't guess types. There's a subtlety, though. If the query string repeats a key, like tag equals a and tag equals b, fromEntries keeps only the last one. Express would give you an array. To be careful, we can write a small loop over the search params that collects repeated keys into arrays.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: I'll do that. It's about six lines, and it avoids silently dropping data, which is the kind of bug that appears in production on a Friday afternoon. Next: req.params. The router returns a params object after matching, and the router middleware assigns it to req.params before calling the handler. We already wrote that in chapter three, so this is just the place where it becomes visible to users. Similarly req.ip comes from socket.remoteAddress. One caution: behind a proxy or load balancer, that address is the proxy's. Real frameworks have a trust proxy setting that reads the X-Forwarded-For header. We'll mention it, but not implement it. Let me wire it all together. In app.js, handle now receives the parsed request and socket, calls createRequest, then creates a response, which we write next lecture, and starts the middleware chain.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Test with a route app.get of slash users slash colon id, whose handler logs req.params.id, req.query and req.get of host. Hit it with curl using a URL with a query string. You should see all three printed correctly. Before we leave, a note on mutation. We're attaching things to req as we go: params from the router, body from the body parser, maybe req.user from an auth middleware. That's the Express model, where req is a shared, mutable bag that middleware decorates. It's flexible, but there's no type safety and no guarantee about what's present. Hono and Koa take different approaches, with a context object. We'll stick with Express style, and in chapter six, plugins will give us a more structured way to add things.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: If req is what we read, res is what we write, and its API is what people use most. Let's create response.js. Think about what a user wants to write. res.status of 201 dot json of an object. res.set of a header. res.send of some text. res.redirect of a URL. They don't want to build header strings by hand like we did in chapter two. Our job is to wrap that raw writing into a chainable, hard-to-misuse object. I'll write a function createResponse, taking the socket and the request, and returning an object with internal state: statusCode, starting at 200, a headers object, and a boolean called headersSent, false at first. Methods return this when it makes sense for chaining. So status takes a code, sets statusCode, and returns the response object.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That's why res.status of 404 dot send of something works. It's a small design decision, called a fluent interface, and it makes code read like a sentence. Next, set. It takes a name and a value, lowercases the name, and stores it. It also accepts an object so you can set several at once, if the first argument is an object. And a matching get, to read back a header you already set. Why lowercase? Same reason as on the request: header names are case-insensitive, and if we lowercase both on the way in, we never get duplicates like Content-Type and content-type, which would be a real bug. When we write the response out, we can send them in lowercase; clients accept that. The central method is end.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: It takes an optional body, a string or a Buffer. First, it converts a string body into a Buffer, with Buffer.from. That gives us the true byte length, remember that trap from chapter two. Then it sets content-length. If headersSent is already true, we throw an error, because writing twice is a bug we want to find loudly. Then it builds the status line, the headers, the blank line, and writes the head and the body to the socket as two writes. Finally it sets headersSent to true. What about the connection itself? If the request said Connection: close, or HTTP 1.0 without keep-alive, we socket.end after the response. Otherwise we leave it open for the next request. That decision lives in end, because it's the moment the response is complete.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: I also add a Date header, since HTTP says servers should send one, and an easy default of Connection: keep-alive. Both are one-liners, and they make our responses look like what browsers expect. Now the reason phrases, which we had as a small object in chapter two. Move it into response.js and add a few more: 204 No Content, 301 Moved Permanently, 302 Found, 304 Not Modified, 401 Unauthorized, 403 Forbidden, 405 Method Not Allowed. If a status isn't in the table, fall back to an empty reason phrase. The HTTP spec actually allows a client to ignore the reason phrase, and HTTP 2 removed it entirely, but HTTP 1.1 still sends it, so we do. Let me show redirect, since it's a nice test of the design.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: res.redirect takes a URL and an optional status, default 302. It sets the location header, sets the status, and calls end with an empty body. Three lines, no new concept, all built on the primitives. That's a good sign for an API: richer methods are tiny compositions of lower-level ones. Try it. Register GET slash old with a handler calling res.redirect of slash new, and curl dash i. You'll see a 302 with a location header. Finally, replace the old writeResponse in server.js with this object, and let the 404 and 500 paths use res too. Our parser's 400 error happens before a res exists, so server.js creates a bare response for that case. Chapter two's raw string writing is gone. We have status, set, get, redirect and end. Next lecture: sending real content types, JSON, HTML and binary.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Now we write the three methods people use all day: res.json, res.html and res.send, and then the one that surprises people, sending binary data. All of them end up calling end from last lecture. The only thing that varies is how we turn a value into bytes and what content-type header we attach. Start with res.json. It takes a value, calls JSON.stringify on it, sets content-type to application slash json with charset utf-8, and calls end with the string. Four lines. There's one trap: JSON.stringify can throw, for instance on a circular reference, or on a BigInt. Because we're inside a middleware pipeline, a thrown error propagates into next with the error, and our error handler sends a 500. That's acceptable.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Another subtle thing is that JSON.stringify of undefined returns undefined, not a string, so a handler calling res.json of undefined would send nothing useful. I'll treat that as null. Next, res.html. Almost identical: set content-type to text slash html with charset utf-8, and call end. I'd like to ask you something. Why is the charset part there? Without it, a browser has to guess how to decode the bytes, and old browsers guess wrong, and you get garbled characters. Always declaring utf-8 removes the guessing. And res.text, similarly, with text slash plain. Notice we're not templating anything, we don't escape anything. If you put user input in HTML, escape it yourself, otherwise you've got cross-site scripting. Now res.send, the shape-shifter. Express's send looks at the type of what you give it.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: A string becomes HTML. A Buffer becomes binary with application slash octet-stream. An object or array becomes JSON. We can do the same with a small switch on typeof. If it's a string, delegate to html, unless a content-type was already set, in which case we respect it. If it's a Buffer, set octet-stream if no type is set and call end. If it's an object, delegate to json. The principle I like here: explicit headers set by the user win over our guesses. Binary is where it gets interesting. Say you want to serve an image. Read the file with fs.readFile, which gives you a Buffer, set the content-type to image slash png, and res.send of the buffer. No string conversion happens, so no corruption.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: A classic bug is converting binary data to a string with toString and back, which mangles bytes outside valid utf-8. By keeping Buffers as Buffers all the way to socket.write, we avoid that whole category of bugs. Test it: send a small PNG and open the URL in your browser. For large files, reading everything into memory is a bad idea. Ten users downloading a one hundred megabyte file would use a gigabyte of RAM. The proper tool is a stream: fs.createReadStream and pipe into the socket. I'll add a method called res.stream, which takes a readable stream, writes the headers without a content-length, and pipes the data. Without a length, we need to either close the connection after the stream, or use chunked encoding.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: In the static file server, in chapter six, we'll know the file size from fs.stat and can send the length. Two small conveniences to finish. res.sendStatus takes a code and sends the reason phrase as the body, so res.sendStatus of 204 and 404 are one-liners. And res.type takes a short name like json or html and maps it to a full mime type, using a tiny lookup. That lookup becomes important in the static server, which needs mime types for dozens of extensions. Let me recap chapter five. Request gives us method, path, query, params, headers and get. Response gives us status, set, json, html, send, redirect and stream. Together with the router and middleware, that's a complete framework core. Everything left is about extending it. And the best way to extend it is a plugin system, which is what the next chapter begins with.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We have a working core. Now the question becomes how people extend it without editing our source. Think about what Express apps do: they call app.use of express.json, app.use of cors, app.use of helmet. Those are all middleware, which already gives us one extension mechanism. But middleware only touches the request pipeline. What if an extension needs to add a method to the app itself, like app.db, or register routes under a prefix, or add several things at once? That's what a plugin system is for, and Fastify built its entire identity around it. Let me define our plugin contract, and keep it tiny. A plugin is a function that takes the app and an options object. It can do anything to the app: call app.use, register routes, attach properties.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: To install one, the user calls app.register of the plugin and an options object. That's it. In app.js, register is two lines: call plugin with app and opts, return app. You might think that's too trivial to be called architecture, but the power is in the convention, because every extension now looks identical. Now the first improvement, which is decorate. Many plugins want to add something reusable to the app, a database client, a logger, a config object. We provide app.decorate, taking a name and a value. It sets app at name to value, but, and this matters, it throws an error if that name already exists. Silent overwrites are how two plugins break each other without telling you. A plugin that depends on another can check app.hasDecorator, and fail early with a clear message.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Let me show it with a tiny plugin. I'll create a file called plugins slash timing.js, exporting a function with app and opts. Inside it calls app.use with a middleware that records Date.now before calling next, and patches res.end to log the elapsed time. Wait, patching is ugly. Better: our middleware pushes a callback, res.onFinish, that our response.js calls at the end of end. Let me add onFinish quickly to response.js: an array of callbacks, run once the response is written. Now the timing plugin is clean. Next, prefixes. Suppose you want a group of routes under slash api slash v1. Fastify lets you register a plugin with the option prefix, and every route inside gets that prefix. We can do that cheaply: register creates a child app object, created with Object.create of the parent, whose get, post and use methods prepend the prefix.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: The plugin receives the child, and doesn't know it's under a prefix. This is encapsulation: the plugin writes slash users, and it ends up registered as slash api slash v1 slash users. Be careful about one thing here. Object.create of app means the child inherits all the parent's properties, but assigning to a property on the child only changes the child. So if a plugin calls decorate on the child, the decoration is visible in that plugin only, and not to sibling plugins. That's exactly the scoping behavior Fastify provides, and it's a feature: a plugin that installs a database client for its own routes doesn't leak it everywhere. Decorations on the root app remain global. What about async setup? Plugins often need to connect to something before the server starts, a database or a config file.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So let's allow plugins to return a promise. register records the promise, and app.listen awaits all pending ones before opening the port. Now a plugin can be async function with await inside, and the server doesn't accept connections until everything is ready. It's the same idea as Fastify's ready, and about five lines of code in listen. Let me summarize the architecture. Middleware transforms the request flow. Decorators add capabilities. Prefixes group routes. Register is the single door through which all of it enters. In the next two lectures we use this system for real, building the two plugins every web framework needs: a body parser, then a static file server. They'll also show whether our plugin design holds up under real work.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: POST requests carry a body, and so far all our framework gives is a Buffer. In createRequest, req.rawBody holds the bytes that the parser read, and req.body is undefined. A body parser turns the bytes into something useful, based on the content-type header. Let's write it as a plugin, in plugins slash bodyParser.js. This is our first real test of the plugin system, so let's see if it behaves. The shape: an exported function taking app and opts. Inside, it calls app.use with a middleware. The middleware looks at req.get of content-type. If the request has no body, meaning rawBody is empty or missing, it calls next and leaves req.body as an empty object. If the content-type starts with application slash json, it parses JSON. If it starts with application slash x-www-form-urlencoded, it parses form fields.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Otherwise, it leaves the body alone, and the handler can use rawBody directly. Let's do JSON first. We write const text equals req.rawBody.toString of utf8, then try JSON.parse of text, assigning the result to req.body. If JSON.parse throws, the client sent invalid JSON, and that's a client mistake, so we create an error with statusCode 400 and the message Invalid JSON, and pass it to next. Our error pipeline from chapter four turns it into a clean 400 response. That's what I wanted you to notice: the earlier design pays off here, since plugin code just calls next of an error and doesn't think about responses. Now the form data. The format is fields separated by ampersands, with each key and value joined by equals, and percent encoding in the values, for example name equals Ada and city equals London.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: URLSearchParams handles this directly, including the plus sign meaning space, and the percent escapes. So the code is Object.fromEntries of new URLSearchParams of text. The same repeated key caveat from the query string applies, and we can reuse the helper from request.js. Let me move that helper into a shared file so both use it, rather than copying it. Limits. This is the part that separates a toy from something I'd trust. A client can send a gigantic body, and we'd buffer it all in memory. So the plugin options include limit, a number of bytes, defaulting to one megabyte. Actually, the best place to enforce the limit is earlier than the plugin, in the parser, before we've buffered more than the maximum.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: So I'll add maxBodySize to the server options, defaulting to one megabyte, and in the parser, if content-length exceeds it, throw an error with status 413, Payload Too Large. The plugin enforces its own tighter limit if provided. Content-Type details also matter. The header can be application slash json, semicolon, charset equals utf-8. So we check startsWith, not equality, or better, strip the parameters first. We also should consider a missing content-type with a body present: most frameworks leave the body alone, and so do we. And what about an empty body with a JSON content-type? JSON.parse of an empty string throws. Many clients send an empty body on a POST, so we treat empty as an empty object rather than an error. Let's test it, with curl.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Send curl dash X POST dash H with content-type application slash json, dash d with a small JSON object, to a route that does res.json of req.body. You get the object back. Send invalid JSON and see a 400. Send form data with dash d name equals Ada and see the fields parsed. Then try a body larger than the limit, which you can generate with head dash c and a big number, and check the 413. One last question: should it be an app-wide middleware or per route? In Express, you can apply express.json to a single route. Our version applies it globally when registered. I'd keep it global, since it's cheap when there's no body. But notice that with prefix scoping from last lecture, registering the plugin inside an api prefix makes it apply only to that group. The plugin system gives us the per-route control for free, which makes me happy about the design.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Last plugin in the course: a static file server. Given a directory, it serves files from it, so a browser can request slash static slash logo.png and get the file. It's a good capstone, because it combines nearly everything: routing with a wildcard, response headers, streaming, error handling, and some real security thinking. Create plugins slash static.js. The plugin takes app and opts, with opts.root being the directory on disk and opts.prefix being the URL prefix. First, it resolves root to an absolute path with path.resolve, once, at setup. Then it registers a GET route for prefix plus slash star. We built wildcards in chapter three, so req.params.star holds whatever came after the prefix, for example images slash logo.png. Should we also respond to HEAD requests? Real servers do, returning headers without a body.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We'll add that as a small bonus at the end. Now the dangerous part, so pay close attention. The user controls req.params.star. If we blindly join it onto the root, a request for slash static slash dot dot slash dot dot slash etc slash passwd would escape the directory and read arbitrary files. This is called path traversal, and it's one of the most common web vulnerabilities. Our defense has two layers. First, decode the path with decodeURIComponent, because attackers encode dots and slashes as percent escapes. Second, compute filePath equals path.join of root and the requested path, and check filePath startsWith root plus path.sep. If it doesn't, respond with 403. Also reject paths containing a null byte.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: A percent 00 in a path can truncate the name in some low-level APIs, and Node actually throws on it, but explicit checks are better than relying on that. I mention this because security bugs in static servers are famous: tons of real packages were patched for exactly this. Our check takes five lines, and I'd rather you internalize why they're there than treat them as magic. Next, find the file. Use fs.promises.stat on filePath inside a try and catch. If it throws with code ENOENT, the file doesn't exist, so we call next, which falls through to our normal 404. If stat says it's a directory, we try index.html inside it. If that's missing too, next again. We don't generate directory listings; that's a privacy and security risk best left to people who ask for it explicitly.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Only regular files get served. Now the response. We know the size from stat, so we can set content-length without buffering anything. The content-type comes from a mime table keyed by file extension: html, css, js, json, png, jpg, svg, txt, and a fallback of application slash octet-stream. Real frameworks use the mime-types package with a database of hundreds; ours is twelve entries, but the mechanism is the same. Then we call res.stream with fs.createReadStream of filePath. Memory use stays flat whether the file is a kilobyte or a gigabyte. Caching gets us the last big win. Build an ETag from the file's size and modification time, for example the hexadecimal of both joined by a dash, and send it as the etag header, along with last-modified.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: When a browser requests the same file again, it sends if-none-match with that value. If it matches, we respond 304 Not Modified with no body. Pages load faster, bandwidth drops, and it costs about six lines. Test it with curl dash i twice and compare. Let's finish by registering it. app.register of the static plugin with root set to public and prefix set to slash static. Put an index.html and an image in public, open the browser, and view them. Try the traversal attack with curl dash dash path-as-is, so curl doesn't normalize the dots, and confirm the 403. We've now built a body parser and a static server entirely as plugins, with no change to the core. That's the proof that the architecture holds. One chapter left, where we step back and compare.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 7.1 - How Fastify Routes 30x Faster than Express
text: For the last chapter we step back from code and ask how Tern compares with the real frameworks, starting with a claim you've probably seen: that Fastify is dozens of times faster than Express. Let's take that apart honestly, because the real story teaches more than the headline does. First, where does the number come from? Fastify's own benchmarks, and independent ones, show Fastify handling roughly two to three times more requests per second than Express in a simple JSON hello world. On a pure routing microbenchmark, with many routes, the gap between a radix tree and a linear scan can be far bigger, and numbers like thirty times show up in specific tests. So be careful: it's true that routing can differ that much, but total application throughput is usually a smaller multiple, since your handler, database and network dominate.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 7.1 - How Fastify Routes 30x Faster than Express
text: Always ask what exactly was measured. So what does Fastify actually do differently? Four things. One: its router, find-my-way, is a radix tree, exactly the structure you built in chapter three, with per-method trees and static children prioritized. Express uses path-to-regexp to compile each route into a regular expression, and walks its layer stack one by one until one matches. Two: Fastify uses a schema for responses. If you declare the shape of your JSON output, it compiles a specialized serializer function, using a library called fast-json-stringify, which beats the generic JSON.stringify. Three: Fastify validates incoming data with a schema compiled to a function, using Ajv, instead of interpreting rules on every request. Four: it avoids work per request.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 7.1 - How Fastify Routes 30x Faster than Express
text: Its request and reply objects are created from prebuilt classes, which keeps V8's hidden classes stable and avoids allocating a new closure per method, the very thing I warned about when we wrote createRequest as a factory. A lot of Fastify's speed is just a long list of small choices that all point the same way: do the work once, at startup, not on every request. Notice the pattern. Our router does the work at registration time and almost none during lookup. Compiling schemas to functions is the same idea. It's a general principle in performance engineering: move computation from the hot path to the setup path. When someone says a framework is fast, the right question is, what did it precompute? Now let's measure Tern.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 7.1 - How Fastify Routes 30x Faster than Express
text: Install autocannon, a Node load-testing tool, with npx autocannon. Write a Tern app with one route returning JSON, and an Express app doing the same, then run autocannon dash c 100 dash d 10 against each. On my machine Tern lands in the same ballpark as Express, a bit slower or faster depending on the day. Please run it yourself, because numbers on a slide are less convincing than numbers on your own terminal. And then add five hundred routes to each and test the last one. That's where the radix tree separates itself. Why wouldn't Tern, which routes fast, win overall? Because of the other costs. Our parser works with strings and allocates per header. We create a response object per request with closures.
