course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
lecture_title: 7.1 - How Fastify Routes 30x Faster than Express
text: We haven't done any tuning on the socket, and we use latin1 string conversion for the head. Node's own http module is backed by llhttp, a parser written in C, which is extremely well tuned. Remember that every framework on Node, Express and Fastify included, sits on that module. Our hand-written parser can't beat it. It was never the point. I want you to leave this lecture with a mindset rather than a number. Benchmarks are tools for finding where time goes. If you profile with node dash dash prof or the Chrome DevTools, you can see what dominates: usually parsing and allocation, not routing. In the next lecture we compare what Express provides that Tern doesn't, which is a long list, and talk about why those features are most of what makes a framework production-ready.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Let's compare Tern and Express feature by feature, and I'll try to be fair to both. The purpose isn't to claim we replaced Express. It's to see which parts of Express you now understand, and which parts remain a black box. We'll go through four categories: what we have in common, what Express has that we don't, what we did differently, and what a production deployment needs. Start with what we share, which is more than you'd expect. The app object with use, get and post. Middleware with next and error handling by function length. Params like colon id. A req with query, params and headers, and a res with status, set, json and send. If you took an Express tutorial from 2015 and swapped the require line for Tern, a surprising amount of it would run.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That's not an accident; the API shape is what made Express so popular, and we copied it knowingly. Now what Express has that we don't. Quite a lot. HTTP 2 and TLS are handled by Node's modules, and we would have to handle them ourselves with the tls module, parsing different framing. Chunked transfer encoding for request bodies. Handling of the Expect: 100-continue header. Pipelining and proper keep-alive timeouts, including slow client protections, such as headers timeout and request timeout, the defense against slowloris attacks. Compression with gzip or brotli. Cookies, sessions, content negotiation with req.accepts, range requests for video, and conditional requests beyond what we did. Then the things we did differently, on purpose. Our router is a radix tree, Express uses a linear stack with regular expressions.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Our plugins have scoping with prefix and decorate, Express routers have mounting but no encapsulation. Our body is parsed by a plugin from a Buffer that the core always reads, while Express leaves the stream untouched until body-parser reads it, which is more memory-friendly for big uploads. Honestly, that last one is a case where Express's choice is better, and I'd redesign Tern to stream bodies in a production version. Express also benefits from time. It was released in 2010 and has had a decade and a half of bug reports, security fixes and edge cases. Remember the static server's path traversal? Express's serve-static, based on the send package, handles ranges, dotfiles, symlinks, weird encodings, caching directives and many bugs that we never thought of. I'm not trying to discourage you.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: I'm showing you that the last ninety percent of a framework is edge cases, and that's the argument for using mature libraries in real work. So when would you actually choose each? For a real product, I'd reach for Fastify if performance and schemas matter, Express if I need the largest ecosystem and familiarity, and Hono if I'm targeting edge runtimes like Cloudflare Workers, since Hono is built on the web standard Request and Response objects rather than Node's sockets. And I'd choose Tern for nothing, which is exactly the right outcome. A good learning project is one you retire. What you do gain from building it is leverage. When Express shows an odd error, you know it came from a middleware that didn't call next.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: When a body arrives empty, you know it's either the order of registration or the content-type. When routing seems slow, you can reason about what a regex stack costs. You can read the Fastify source, find-my-way or Hono's router, and recognise the pieces. Debugging is mostly about having an accurate mental model, and now yours is. Before the last lecture, one exercise. Pick one thing from the list that Tern lacks, and add it. Cookie parsing is a great start, a plugin that reads the cookie header into req.cookies and adds res.cookie. Or gzip with the zlib module. Or request timeouts. Each is a plugin, a few dozen lines, and each will teach you a part of HTTP that we skipped. Next time, we wrap up the whole course and look at where to go.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: We've reached the end, so let's look back at what we built and where you can take it. Open your tern folder and look at the file list. server.js, which owns the TCP sockets and the connection loop. parser.js, which turns bytes into a request. router.js, the radix tree with params and wildcards. app.js, with use, register, decorate and the middleware dispatcher. request.js and response.js for the friendly objects. And the plugins folder, with a body parser and a static file server. A framework, in a few hundred lines. Let me trace one request through the whole thing, from start to end, because that's the real summary of the course. A browser opens a TCP connection, and net.createServer hands us a socket.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Bytes arrive in data events, and we append them to a buffer. parseRequest looks for the blank line, reads the request line and headers, waits for the body per content-length, and returns a parsed object. createRequest and createResponse wrap it. Then dispatch runs the middleware stack, with next stepping through it, and error handling when something throws. Midway, the body parser plugin turns rawBody into req.body. Finally the router looks up the method's tree, walks the radix nodes, extracts params, and calls our handler. The handler calls res.json, which stringifies, sets headers, and calls end, which writes the status line, headers, blank line and body to the socket. And the socket stays open for the next request.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: That entire journey is the answer to the question we started with: how does an HTTP request become a response? Here's what I hope you take away, beyond the code. First, HTTP is just text on a stream, and every framework feature is a convenience on top. Second, data structures decide performance: the radix tree beat the list because it moved work to registration time. Third, small, composable abstractions, middleware and plugins, are what keep frameworks extensible without growing a thousand options. And fourth, security and limits are a design concern from day one, as we saw with body size and path traversal. If you want to keep going, here's a roadmap. Add chunked transfer encoding for both requests and responses. Add timeouts for headers and idle connections.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Add cookies and sessions as plugins. Then add compression, then CORS, then rate limiting. After that, try a bigger leap: swap net for tls to support HTTPS, and read about how HTTP 2 multiplexes streams on one connection, which changes the parser completely. HTTP 3 moves to QUIC over UDP, a different universe again. On the reading side, I'd recommend the source of Fastify and find-my-way, which is readable, and the Hono source, which is small and shows a framework built on web standards. Read RFC 9110 and 9112, the modern HTTP specs, since they're clearer than their reputation. And read the llhttp repository to see how a state-machine parser handles all the cases that our split and indexOf calls ignore.

course_title: Build a Web Framework from Scratch
text: Try to find three places where our parser would misbehave, and fix them. Also consider polishing Tern into a portfolio piece. Add tests with Node's built-in test runner, node colon test. Write a README showing the architecture. Publish a benchmark with honest methodology. Employers and teammates love seeing that you understand your tools from the ground up, and a framework from scratch says it better than any line on a resume. Thank you for building this with me. You started with an empty folder and a question, and you now have a working framework, a radix tree you wrote yourself, and a mental model that makes Express, Fastify and Hono make sense. Keep experimenting, keep breaking things, and the next time something in your stack seems magical, remember that it's probably just a socket, a buffer, and a carefully chosen data structure. Happy building.
